thread_1.topic_name: Non-Canonical Price Feeds Allow Historical Price Manipulation

sources.title: Non-Canonical Price Feeds Allow Historical Price Manipulation
sources.evidence_text:
Non-Canonical Price Feeds Allow Historical Price Manipulation
We found that the protocol does **not enforce canonical accounts** for `sol_usd_pyth_feed` . Any account with the same `feed ID` can be submitted, allowing anyone to create a `PriceUpdateV2` account and publish historical prices. For example, with a 5-minute age window:

- Transaction 1 uses price `t2` (latest).

- Transaction 2 uses price `t1` (older, t1 < t2) from a custom account.

While the protocol correctly validates publish and update times, this issue allows users to submit historical valid prices within the allowed time window (which was configured to be 60s), potentially manipulating outcomes.
- Use a **canonical feed account** managed and sponsored by Pyth.

- Alternatively, use a **personal, persistent account** that you control and update yourself.

thread_3.topic_name: Anyone can dust a stake vault and permanently block unstaking

sources.title: Anyone can dust a stake vault and permanently block unstaking
sources.evidence_text:
Anyone can dust a stake vault and permanently block unstaking
`unstake` transfers only the principal recorded in `StakeAccount` and then unconditionally closes the vault, even though the vault can receive unsolicited token transfers. Any holder of the pool mint can send one base unit to a victim’s publicly derivable vault; the resulting nonzero remainder makes `CloseAccount` fail and atomically rolls back every withdrawal attempt, while no instruction can sweep the excess.
In step 1, transfer the full token account balance to the staker, instead of the recorded balance.

# Supply Chain Compromise

##### Sub-techniques (3)

Adversaries may manipulate products or product delivery mechanisms prior to receipt by a final consumer for the purpose of data or system compromise.

Supply chain compromise can take place at any stage of the supply chain including:

* Manipulation of development tools
* Manipulation of a development environment
* Manipulation of source code repositories (public or private)
* Manipulation of source code in open-source dependencies
* Manipulation of software update/distribution mechanisms
* Compromised/infected system images (removable media infected at the factory)[[1]](https://www-01.ibm.com/support/docview.wss?uid=ssg1S1010146&myns=s028&mynp=OCSTHGUJ&mynp=OCSTLM5A&mynp=OCSTLM6B&mynp=OCHW206&mync=E&cm_sp=s028-_-OCSTHGUJ-OCSTLM5A-OCSTLM6B-OCHW206-_-E)[[2]](https://www.se.com/us/en/download/document/SESN-2018-236-01/)
* Replacement of legitimate software with modified versions
* Sales of modified/counterfeit products to legitimate distributors
* Shipment interdiction

While supply chain compromise can impact any component of hardware or software, adversaries looking to gain execution have often focused on malicious additions to legitimate software in software distribution or update channels.[[3]](https://blog.avast.com/new-investigations-in-ccleaner-incident-point-to-a-possible-third-stage-that-had-keylogger-capacities)[[4]](https://cloudblogs.microsoft.com/microsoftsecure/2018/03/07/behavior-monitoring-combined-with-machine-learning-spoils-a-massive-dofoil-coin-mining-campaign/)[[5]](https://web.archive.org/web/20160309235002/https://www.commandfive.com/papers/C5_APT_SKHack.pdf) Adversaries may limit targeting to a desired victim set or distribute malicious software to a broad set of consumers but only follow up with specific victims.[[6]](https://web.archive.org/web/20190717233006/http:/www.symantec.com/content/en/us/enterprise/media/security_response/whitepapers/the-elderwood-project.pdf)[[3]](https://blog.avast.com/new-investigations-in-ccleaner-incident-point-to-a-possible-third-stage-that-had-keylogger-capacities)[[5]](https://web.archive.org/web/20160309235002/https://www.commandfive.com/papers/C5_APT_SKHac

July 2026 TRANSACTION SHAPE & NEW ARCHITECTURE REQUIREMENTS JULY 2026 JULY 2026 1.1 Defining Agentic Commerce Agentic commerce is a new economic surface where software autonomously discovers, evaluates, and executes transactions  continuously, programmatically, and across a far wider range of commerce than traditional payment infrastructure was designed to handle. The degree of autonomy varies. Some workflows keep a human in the loop to review or approve purchases, while others run fully autonomously once configured. Agents can buy SaaS licenses, book travel, automate accounts payable, reorder physical inventory, and commission creative work, often without human intervention at the moment of purchase. Within that broader landscape, a new sub-category of machine-native, sub-dollar transactions is also emerging: an AI agent calls an API, receives an HTTP 402 response (Payment Required), evaluates the price, pays, and consumes the resource. That cycle takes milliseconds and requires no checkout page, saved card, or browsing session  only a wallet or card, a budget, and an objective. For payment providers, the full spectrum of agentic commerce creates new transaction surfaces with different economics, risk controls, and infrastructure requirements from traditional e-commerce.
AI crosses the line from chatbot to agent when it begins to reason through multi-step tasks, call external tools, evaluate results, and iterate on its approach autonomously. Agents built on frontier models like Claude, GPT, and Gemini are now deployed in production across every business vertical. Over the past year, these agents have become very capable at writing code and conducting research, but they are inherently limited by access.
Giving agents the ability to pay removes that constraint: An IT agent purchases fifty additional seats on a SaaS platform after headcount changes.
An administrative agent reorders printer toner and breakroom supplies when inventory runs low.
A research agent queries five financial data providers a few cents each for the same company’s filings, then picks the most complete dataset.
A marketing agent pays ten image-generation providers 5 cents each to render the same product shot, then selects the best output.
Agentic payments span two distinct transaction categories. The first is macro, where an agent executes high-value, consumer-like purchases on behalf of a human (e.g., booking travel, managing subscriptions, ordering supplies). These transactions resemble traditional e-commerce, with the agent acting as a proxy for human intent. The second category is micro, characterized by high-frequency, low-value purchases (i.e., API calls, data queries, compute access, tool usage) initiated by the agent. Both categories are real and growing, but micro-transactions are the area where new payment architecture is most needed, and where new protocols are emerging to fill the gap.

# Agentic Payments

Machine-to-machine onchain payment activity across open HTTP 402 payment standards — x402 and MPP (onchain Tempo rails only).

The `payments.agentic_payments` table captures machine-to-machine onchain payment activity settled through open payment standards built on HTTP 402. The dataset covers two protocols:

* **x402** — an onchain-native payment standard. Payment settlement is fully trackable onchain via facilitator infrastructure.
* **MPP (Machine Payments Protocol)** — supports both onchain and offchain payment methods; this dataset tracks only its onchain Tempo rails: Tempo Charge (one-time onchain payments) and Tempo Session (onchain escrow and settlement, with offchain usage metering between onchain events).

Each row represents one onchain payment settlement — order creation, authorization, and intermediate protocol events that do not themselves settle onchain are excluded. Agentic payments feed into `payments.commerce_flows` as a Tier A (label-based) source, classified as `party_pair = b2b`, `purpose = commerce`, `confidence = high`.

## Why this dataset matters

Agentic payments let AI agents and automated services pay each other onchain without human involvement. Tracking them separately makes it possible to:

* Measure the scale and growth of machine-to-machine payment activity.
* Attribute stablecoin transfers to specific agentic protocols (x402, MPP).
* Compare protocol adoption across chains and over time.

## [​](#coverage) Coverage

**Protocols:** x402, MPP (onchain Tempo rails only). **Chains:** Base, Polygon, and Solana (x402); Tempo (MPP). **Tokens:** Not restricted to stablecoins — x402 rows can include EIP-3009 tokens (e.g. USDC, EURC), other ERC-20 tokens, and classic SPL token transfers on Solana. `settlement_pattern` is currently enriched only for decoded USDC EIP-3009 transfers on EVM; Permit2 and Solana settlement decoding are future phases. Native SOL and Token-2022 are not covered yet (excluded follow-ups). **x402 facilitators** are tracked via `facilitator_name`. New facilitators are added as they appear onchain.
